strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in GNN benchmarking by proposing a methodology to isolate structural understanding from feature information, which is well-motivated and novel
Methodologically sound with correct equivariance proofs (Theorem A.1), flexible dataset generation handling diverse graph topologies, and well-justified BFS sampling for large graphs

Comprehensive experimental validation across 40 datasets with rigorous statistical reporting (10 runs, error bars), multiple architecture comparisons, and extensive baseline comparisons for positional encodings
Impressive practical results: achieves state-of-the-art on PCQM4Mv2 (MAE 0.0337) with only 37.9M parameters compared to 47M-203M for competitors
Strong insight that performance at optimal noise level generalizes across all noise levels, providing practical guidance
Excellent reproducibility: open-source Python package, public datasets, detailed hyperparameters, and specified compute requirements enable community use
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental - primarily adapts Nowak et al. [2017] to different graph topologies rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts
Critical parameter (noise level η) selection is task and architecture-specific with no principled a priori method, severely limiting practical applicability and contradicting generalizability claims
Connection between graph alignment performance and downstream task performance is assumed rather than rigorously validated - tested on only 2-3 molecular tasks without broader domain exploration
GAPE generation requires knowing the best architecture beforehand (Table F.7), creating circular dependency that limits practical utility
Unfair baseline comparisons: SPE and PEARL methods fail with OOM errors rather than being genuinely outperformed; no memory-efficient alternatives attempted
Limited theoretical understanding of why learned positional encodings from graph alignment outperform spectral methods, and what structural properties GAPE captures
Paper tries to cover three distinct contributions (benchmarking, positional encodings, SOTA results) making it feel unfocused; positional encoding work feels disconnected and somewhat superficial
Inconsistent experimental setup: benchmarking uses 20K/2K split of PCQM4Mv2 while SOTA results use full dataset, making it unclear whether improvements come from the encoding or scale
Heavy computational cost for GAPE generation (~2.5 hours for PCQM4Mv2) compared to closed-form spectral methods, but this trade-off is not discussed

Limited analysis of why anisotropic architectures outperform isotropic ones despite claiming this demonstrates 'finer structural understanding' - no ablation studies or attention visualization provided

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly articulates a gap in GNN benchmarking—isolating structural understanding from feature understanding rather than conflating both
Practical methodological contribution: extends graph alignment benchmarking from Erdős-Rényi graphs to arbitrary topologies with noise-controlled difficulty, enabling multi-domain evaluation
Strong reproducibility: comprehensive experimental details, error bars over 10 runs, detailed hyperparameters, and open-source Python package with code and dataset generation tools
Empirical breadth: evaluates multiple perspectives including architecture benchmarking, optimal noise analysis, positional encoding comparisons on three datasets, and SOTA results on PCQM4Mv2
Clear presentation of core idea and well-structured paper with extensive appendices documenting experimental setup
weaknesses: Limited core algorithmic novelty: the siamese graph alignment architecture is from Nowak et al. (2017); the main contribution is adapting it to different topologies via noise perturbations, which is engineering-focused and incremental

Insufficient theoretical justification for core claims: (1) why should graph alignment specifically measure 'structural understanding'? This connection is assumed not established; (2) the 'optimal noise' phenomenon is observed empirically but lacks theoretical explanation; (3) the noise parameter's ability to uniformly control difficulty across diverse topologies is validated on only 5 datasets without principled analysis

Ad-hoc dataset generation methodology: the noise-based edge perturbation strategy lacks principled justification; two different p_add/p_remove strategies depending on density appear unmotivated; BFS sampling for large graphs introduces unvalidated approximations to the benchmark

Limited benchmarking scope and claims: only 5 base datasets (all small, ~14-100 nodes); only 1-WL MPNN architectures; comparison largely among similar models (GCN, GIN, GAT variants); generalization across noise levels claimed but Figure 3 shows substantial scatter suggesting limited validity

Mixed and potentially unfair GAPE results: GAPE alone underperforms on ZINC (0.147 vs SignNet 0.116); requires combination with RWPE to achieve best results; compared against strictly more expressive positional encodings (1-WL vs higher expressivity) creating asymmetric comparison; performance highly sensitive to pre-training dataset (Table E.5) suggesting poor transfer

SOTA claims lack proper rigor: Table 2 conflates parameter count differences (6.2M–37.9M vs 19.4M–203M), feature usage (2D only vs bonds/atoms), and domain preprocessing; only 2 runs reported; no ablations isolating GAPE's independent contribution; task-specific pre-training on PCQM4Mv2 then evaluation on same dataset is somewhat circular

Weak validation of core assumption: no empirical evidence beyond 3 molecular datasets that graph alignment performance predicts downstream task performance; the connection between alignment quality and GNN expressivity is inferred not proven

Generalization claims unsupported: Figure E.1 shows only within-distribution generalization (across noise levels); out-of-distribution transfer to novel graph families untested; Table E.5 shows substantial degradation with mismatched pre-training datasets

Presentation scope issues: paper attempts to cover benchmarking, positional encodings, and SOTA simultaneously without sufficient depth in any area; vague claims like 'anisotropic architectures enable finer understanding'; non-informative Figure 1

Missing experimental validations: no comparison with PATTERN/CLUSTER datasets from prior work; no ablation on design choices (loss function, algorithm for permutation extraction); no statistical significance testing on SOTA results; standard deviations sometimes large (GIN Erdős-Rényi 12%: 54.8±4.2)

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in GNN evaluation by separating structural understanding from feature understanding through graph alignment
Sound theoretical framework with Theorem A.1 properly establishing equivariance properties of the siamese algorithm
Comprehensive experimental validation: 40 datasets, 10 runs per experiment, consistent results across noise levels, proper error reporting
Impressive practical results: state-of-the-art on PCQM4Mv2 (0.0337 MAE) using 37.9M parameters vs. competitors with 77-203M
Excellent reproducibility: open-source package, all hyperparameters specified, public datasets, detailed appendix
Novel insight about optimal noise levels maximizing performance gaps, enabling more robust architecture ranking
Well-designed dataset generation methodology with two variants handling different graph topologies appropriately
Clear, well-written presentation with effective motivation and good use of figures
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification for why graph alignment performance should transfer to downstream tasks beyond intuitive topology sharing arguments
GAPE positional encodings are dataset-specific, performing best when pre-trained on matching topologies (Table E.5), limiting generalizability as claimed
Optimal noise level is data-dependent with no principled selection method, requiring empirical determination and adding implicit tuning
Some empirical results are predictable from existing theory (anisotropic > isotropic from Weisfeiler-Lehman expressivity), limiting conceptual novelty
Laplacian baseline performance is poorly explained; unclear why training-free method performs so poorly despite being standard
Limited comparison to other structural understanding benchmarks (PATTERN/CLUSTER dismissed but not compared)
Only 5 base datasets tested—unclear if results generalize to other graph domains (knowledge graphs, biological networks, etc.)
Paper attempts two substantial contributions (benchmarking + positional encodings) somewhat diluting focus and clarity
SOTA comparison uses simple transformer; unclear if this architecture is optimal for comparing different positional encoding methods
Missing ablation studies on whether residual connections/GraphNorm or architectural innovations drive performance differences

strengths: Novel methodology for generating graph alignment datasets from arbitrary graph topologies with controllable difficulty levels, enabling structure-only benchmarking without feature confounds
Rigorous theoretical framework with well-formulated equivariance theorems (A.1, B.2, C.1) that properly handle graph automorphisms and prove consistency of the siamese architecture
Comprehensive experimental validation: 40 datasets, 5 architectures, 8 noise levels, 10 runs each with careful statistical analysis and reproducibility details
Key empirical finding that optimal task difficulty produces statistically significant performance gaps that generalize across noise levels—this insight has important practical implications
Convincing evidence that learned embeddings capture structural information: 98%+ edge reconstruction accuracy and strong negative correlation with downstream tasks (r < −0.90)
GAPE positional encodings achieve competitive or superior performance compared to existing methods on molecular regression tasks without access to edge features
Open-source package commitment and extensive appendices with implementation details, hyperparameters, and additional experiments enhance reproducibility
weaknesses: Critical theoretical gap: Theoretical guarantees for optimal alignment (Table C.1) exist only for Erdős-Rényi graphs; for other topologies (AQSOL, PCQM4Mv2, etc.), no verification that planted solutions are actually optimal, potentially invalidating benchmark conclusions

Optimal noise level η* lacks theoretical justification—purely empirically observed with large variations across datasets (12%-18%), and authors provide no principled method to select η* for new datasets a priori

Limited novelty relative to foundational work: Siamese architecture and correlation-based dataset generation from Nowak et al. (2017); main contribution is extending to arbitrary topologies, which is somewhat incremental
Scope restrictions: Main benchmarking limited to 1-WL expressive models; higher-order GNN results (Section H) relegated to appendix despite being important for expressivity hierarchy

GAPE positional encodings inherently limited by 1-WL expressivity while competing methods (RWPE, SignNet, GPSE) exceed 1-WL power; GAPE+RWPE outperforms GAPE alone (Table 1), indicating fundamental limitations
No direct empirical comparison with existing benchmarks (OGB, TUDataset): Missing evidence that model rankings on graph alignment correlate with rankings on established benchmarks
Practical scalability limited to ~10,000 vertices without subsampling; BFS sampling preserves local topology but potential bias for power-law networks not thoroughly analyzed
Multiple unjustified design choices: BCE loss vs. alternatives, 64-dimensional embeddings, two noise parameterizations not compared, hyperparameter sensitivity not explored

strengths: Clear methodology for generating graph alignment datasets from arbitrary graphs with controllable difficulty levels
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 40 datasets with 5 base domains and multiple architectures (10 runs each)
Theoretical grounding provided through equivariance theorems (A.1, B.2) and connection to WL hierarchy (Theorem C.1)
Extensive experimental details, hyperparameter specifications, and attention to reproducibility
Multiple validation approaches including downstream task correlation (r < -0.9), graph reconstruction (98% accuracy), and comparison with existing positional encodings
Well-organized presentation with clear problem formulation and thorough appendices
weaknesses: Critical methodological issue: Planted solutions are only guaranteed optimal below certain noise thresholds (e.g., η ≤ 30% for AQSOL), yet models train/test at higher noise levels, potentially matching against suboptimal targets—this undermines confidence in learned comparisons
No theoretical justification for why optimal noise must exist; optimal noise varies by dataset (12%-18%) with no principled selection method, making the benchmark less principled than claimed

Overclaimed and unfocused contributions: Benchmarking results mainly confirm existing knowledge (anisotropic > isotropic GNNs); GAPE positional encodings underperform baselines when used alone and require dataset-matched pretraining, suggesting learned representations are dataset-specific rather than universal
Limited novelty: Core contribution is adapting Nowak et al. (2017) to multiple graph types and adding noise parameter; most interpretations (metric learning, denoising) are straightforward
Unclear practical impact: Benchmarking reveals no new architectural insights; GAPE only works best when combined with RWPE (Table 1) and requires careful dataset selection (Table K.11)
Fundamental optimality concern inadequately addressed: Section C.1 shows planted solutions may not be truly optimal at tested noise levels, creating invalid learning targets
Scalability severely limited to graphs < 10,000 nodes; BFS sampling may not preserve global structure properties critical for the alignment task
Experimental anomalies: Very small standard deviations (e.g., 99.8 ± 0.0) raise questions about validation; different noise schedules for different tasks appear ad-hoc
Incomplete comparisons: No head-to-head comparison with PATTERN/CLUSTER/CSL showing correlation superiority; limited comparison with neural algorithmic reasoning benchmarks
Paper tries to cover too much ground (benchmarking + positional encodings), diluting both contributions; neither stands alone as sufficiently compelling

strengths: Novel benchmarking methodology addressing genuine gap: structure-only evaluation applicable to diverse graph topologies without modifying them, filling space between feature-centric benchmarks and limited-topology synthetic benchmarks

Rigorous theoretical foundation: proper treatment of automorphisms (Theorems B.2), equivariance properties (Theorem A.1), and connection to Weisfeiler-Leman expressivity with formal bounds (Theorem C.1)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 40 datasets across 5 base graph types with 8 noise levels, 10 runs per config with proper error reporting, consistent findings across 5+ architectures, additional validation with higher-order GNNs

Key practical insight that optimal task difficulty exists where statistical separation maximizes; demonstrated that performance rankings generalize across noise levels when trained at η*, valuable for practitioners

GAPE application is novel and effective: achieves competitive or superior performance vs. more expressive positional encodings (Table 1), near-perfect graph reconstruction (>94% F1) indicating meaningful structure compression, strong correlation with downstream tasks (r < -0.90)

Excellent reproducibility: extensive appendices with complete hyperparameters, clear algorithms, dataset specifications, reasonable training times (20-40 min), promise of open-source code with sufficient detail for reimplementation
Clear presentation with logical flow; Table C.2 provides valuable comparison distinguishing this work from existing combinatorial benchmarks; honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Fundamental limitation to 1-WL message-passing architectures: framework cannot benchmark more expressive GNN families (subgraph methods, higher-order GNNs are tested but not integrated into core methodology), limiting utility as architectures evolve

Planted solution optimality not guaranteed for real graphs: theoretical guarantees only for Erdös-Rényi; Table C.1 bounds restrict η < 30% for most datasets to preserve optimality, yet no empirical validation that planted solutions remain optimal at higher noise levels, undermining claims about difficulty control

Limited downstream evaluation: GAPE tested only on molecular regression (3 datasets); no validation on other domains (citation networks, knowledge graphs, social networks); strong dataset selection effects (Table K.11) without systematic guidance for choosing pre-training dataset

Optimal noise level η* still requires dataset-specific tuning despite claims of transferability; different η values needed across datasets (12-18%); no principled method to select η a priori for new datasets, partially undermining practical utility claims

Insufficient statistical rigor: standard deviations reported but no hypothesis testing; cases in Figure 3 show overlapping error bars yet models are ranked; no confidence intervals or significance testing for claimed differences

Limited mechanistic insight: paper demonstrates anisotropic > isotropic on structure but lacks deep analysis of why; denoising interpretation (C.4) is speculative; no ablation studies on architecture components (residual connections, GraphNorm, etc.)

Incomplete benchmarking comparisons: Laplacian baseline is training-free (unfair comparison); no transfer studies showing whether models trained on PATTERN/CLUSTER transfer to Graph Alignment; missing head-to-head comparisons on common ground

Scalability concerns: O(N²) similarity matrix and O(N³) Hungarian algorithm limit applicability; BFS sampling for large graphs modifies the problem; no experiments on >100k node graphs; practical applicability to modern large-scale settings unclear
